spoof

SPOOF -- one syllable, rhymes with 'roof.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Spoof is a humorous imitation of a work, style, or genre.

The magazine's annual spoof issue imitates a serious newspaper, right down to a fake weather report.

Example

For the film festival, three eighth graders shoot a nature documentary about their own school: a hushed voice-over tracks 'the wild freshman in its natural habitat,' dramatic music swells over the cafeteria line, and a slow-motion shot follows a paper airplane like a migrating bird.

Their film is a spoof: a humorous imitation of an entire genre -- the nature documentary -- with all its familiar features lovingly copied and made ridiculous. A spoof mocks the style itself: the hushed narration, the swelling music, the slow-motion wildlife shots.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

takeoff: A takeoff is a quick, light riff on a familiar style -- playful, casual, often over in a moment. A spoof commits further: it imitates a whole work or genre from start to finish, copying its familiar features to make them ridiculous.

impression: An impression imitates one person: a comedian borrows a celebrity's voice, walk, and catchphrases for a minute on stage. A spoof aims wider, imitating a whole work, genre, or style -- the format itself is the joke, not any single individual.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

tribute: a work made to honor something sincerely

salute: a gesture of genuine respect and admiration

Where it sits · how harshly the target is mocked — send-up → spoof → lampoon

send-up vs. spoof: A send-up is gentler than a spoof: it affectionately teases a genre it clearly loves, while a spoof mocks its target's habits more sharply and openly.

lampoon vs. spoof: Lampoon is the strongest and sharpest: a spoof or send-up pokes fun, but a lampoon attacks -- its laughter is meant to leave a mark on its target.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — spoof

root — spoof: a game of hoaxing and trickery (invented by British comedian Arthur Roberts in the 1880s)

Put it together

Put it together: Spoof has no ancient roots at all -- it was simply made up. In the 1880s, the British comedian Arthur Roberts invented a parlor game of tricks and bluffing and called it 'Spoof.' The name jumped from the game to any hoax, and then settled on the friendly kind of hoax we know today: a work that playfully imitates another for laughs.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Spoof has no root to pass along because it never had one: the British comedian Arthur Roberts simply invented the word in the 1880s as the name of his parlor game of tricks and bluffing. A made-up word has no family tree, so there is no relative to hunt for.

Strength Check

Word Choice

A spoof imitates a whole work, genre, or style -- a spoof of spy movies, of cooking shows, of a solemn newspaper. Keep it apart from its unit-mate caricature, which comically inflates the distinctive features of one specific person or thing, usually in a drawing. If the joke copies a format, it is a spoof; if the joke inflates somebody's chin or eyebrows, it is a caricature.
